title: Sample complexity of symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
formal: Determine the minimax trajectory-length complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) of identity testing for symmetric Markov chains in the model below, up to universal multiplicative constants. Both the state-space size \(n\) and reciprocal proximity \(1/\varepsilon\) vary. Give an explicit positive comparison function \(B(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[cB(n,\varepsilon)\le M(n,\varepsilon)\le CB(n,\varepsilon)\] for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). Constants must be independent of the reference chain, the starting state, \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\); logarithmic factors in these parameters may not be suppressed. If the complexity is infinite on part of this domain, identify that part and prove infinitude there instead of assigning it a finite bound.
why: This asks how much dependent data is needed to validate an entire stochastic transition rule when the experiment cannot be restarted or directed toward unvisited states. Sharp bounds would separate the intrinsic information cost of testing dynamics from the cost of fully exploring the reference chain, extending the foundations of distribution testing beyond independent samples.
status_note: Source-open as the optimal trajectory-complexity question in COLT 2018 Section 6. On 15 September 2026, the full original model and bounds, the 2019 irreducibility convention and theorem, and the 2022/2023 reversible extensions were checked. A bounded later-work search did not identify matching joint bounds for the retained full symmetric model. progress.text: The COLT paper defines the single-trajectory spectral-discrepancy model, proves a hitting-time-dependent upper bound and an \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\) lower bound, and proposes \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) in its first open question.

Cherapanamjeri–Bartlett Theorem 10 gives a \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) tester under the irreducible symmetric setting stated in Section 2.1; the conclusion retains the optimal reciprocal-distance dependence as an open question.
Fried–Wolfer extend testing to irreducible reversible chains under a stationary-distribution proximity promise. Their symmetric specialization recovers the \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) scale.
Wolfer–Watanabe give a geometric reduction under additional conditions, explicitly separating this discrepancy-based problem from testing under the matrix infinity norm.

importance.reason: A foundational dependent-data testing problem with a single uncontrolled trajectory, a carefully motivated spectral discrepancy and a substantial unresolved joint parameter gap. It probes whether validation needs global exploration and connects information-theoretic testing with Markov dynamics.

sentences: The tester observes one trajectory from an unknown symmetric Markov chain and receives a complete known reference transition matrix.
It must distinguish equality from positive spectral discrepancy for every uncontrolled starting state, without resets or chosen-state sampling.
The target is matching joint dependence of the worst-case required trajectory length on the number of states and the proximity parameter.
Later testing results remove hitting-time dependence under their stated irreducibility assumptions, but the checked bounds still leave a reciprocal-distance gap.
The card preserves the full original symmetric model and distinguishes its transition discrepancy from stationary-distribution or matrix-norm testing.

definitions: A chain on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has a transition matrix \(P\in[0,1]^{n\times n}\) with \(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). Symmetry means \(P_{ij}=P_{ji}\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros, holding probabilities and disconnected state spaces are allowed. For two such matrices set \[R(P,Q)_{ij}=\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}},\qquad \Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho(R(P,Q)),\] where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius, the maximum absolute value of an eigenvalue. The square root is entrywise; it is not a matrix square root. The resulting discrepancy lies in \([0,1]\), but it need not be a metric. The tester receives \(n\), rational \(\varepsilon\), the complete reference matrix \(Q\), and observations from one trajectory of an unknown symmetric matrix \(P\). For every initial state \(x\in[n]\), \(X_0=x\) and \[\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_t]=P_{X_t,j}.\] The tester sees \(X_0\) without a transition cost; each subsequent observed transition costs one. It cannot choose the initial state, reset the chain, request a transition from an arbitrary state, or inspect entries of \(P\). It may stop early, but it must stop within the claimed worst-case number of transitions. It accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(P=Q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(\Delta(P,Q)>\varepsilon\), for every starting state. No guarantee is imposed for other unequal pairs. Probabilities include both the Markov trajectory and independent internal fair random bits. Correctness for every fixed starting state also covers every starting distribution. The tester is one finite uniform program across all \(n,\varepsilon,Q\), with integer and bit-string work storage and exact real registers holding the supplied entries of \(Q\). It has rational constants, exact arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) with division by zero forbidden, nonnegative square root, and exact order/equality comparisons; it has no advice or other oracle. The integer and rational parameters use binary encodings. These conventions specify exact numerical access; no bit-time guarantee for arbitrary real input is being requested. Local computation, memory and access to the explicitly supplied \(Q\) are uncharged, but every execution terminates. For each \(n,\varepsilon\), let \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(m\) attained as a worst-case transition bound by a uniform tester correct for every permitted parameter value, reference and unknown chain. The worst case includes every \(Q,P\), starting state and execution. Set \(M=+\infty\) if no finite bound exists. This is a worst-reference minimax quantity, rather than a reference-dependent hitting-time or mixing-time complexity. The full symmetric class in the original boxed problem is retained; irreducibility, aperiodicity and stationary initialization are not extra promises.
answer_criterion: Supply the comparison function and a complete Lean-checked proof of the matching bounds, including correctness and trajectory cost of one uniform upper-bound tester and a lower bound against every tester in the stated model. Any asserted infinite values require a Lean proof that no finite uniform bound exists there. Merely repeating the defining minimization, suppressing unbounded logarithmic factors, or proving a bound only for fast-mixing or irreducible inputs does not meet the full target. The source's proposed \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) answer is a conjectured value of this complexity, not an assumption that an accepted answer must confirm.

source_formulation.text: Determine the optimal sample complexity for identity testing of symmetric Markov chains; the source proposes order n/epsilon and asks whether explicit hitting-time dependence can be removed.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 6, item 1

context_blocks.text: Independent distribution samples can be collected from scratch. Here the next observation is constrained by the current state, so revisiting an uninformative region may consume many observations. The reference matrix is fully known; only the transition rule that generated the trajectory is unknown.

A worst-case start makes some unequal chains indistinguishable: they may share a closed component with identical transitions, and the trajectory may never leave it. The source chooses a spectral discrepancy that vanishes in such cases. Replacing it with a maximum row distance would impose rejection obligations that a single trajectory might never be able to meet.

The square-root overlap matrix compares both transition rules on the same labeled state space. Its leading spectral behavior measures how quickly the distributions of long trajectories can separate. Testing equality of stationary distributions alone would not test this object; in particular, symmetric chains all admit the uniform stationary distribution.

The original sample complexity is trajectory length in observed states. This card counts transitions after the initial state, a difference of one. It retains the original strict farness inequality and asks for matching joint dependence on state count and proximity, with constants and the minimax reference convention made explicit.

The original upper bound includes a reference hitting-time term, and its lower bound is \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\). The hitting time is the largest expected time to reach a specified state from another state; it may be very large or infinite. Section 6 conjectures that a matching order-\(n/\varepsilon\) bound should avoid that dependence.

The 2019 paper removes hitting-time dependence in its stated irreducible symmetric setting, with bound \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\). Its Section 5 still asks whether the reciprocal-distance gap can be closed. This review records the irreducibility assumption from Section 2.1 rather than silently treating that theorem as an unrestricted statement about every reducible input.

Later work extends this line to reversible chains with additional stationary-distribution conditions, and develops a geometric reduction. Those extensions address broader types of transition matrix under promises; the checked results do not establish matching joint bounds for the full original symmetric problem.

Bounds in a matrix norm, experiments with a controlled restart interface, or results stated after assuming stationary initialization solve distinct testing problems. The source also asks other questions about its discrepancy and more general chains; those directions are not additional targets of this card.
